summary: This session builds on a prior talk about MCP giving LLMs access to CAPTCHA-protected sites. The core thesis is that scraping is no longer the hard part—maintaining scrapers is. Instead of asking an LLM to parse every page (prohibitively expensive in tokens), Bright Data's skill sets teach an LLM to build a production scraper that parses pages via script. The demo uses Claude Code with Bright Data's GitHub-hosted skills and connected MCP. The agent fetches skills, extracts HTML or markdown via MCP, identifies selectors, and generates a working scraper in minutes. Scrape-as-markdown mode returns only page text to save tokens, and JSON output is even more token-efficient than markdown. The MCP exposes 66 tools: curl-style URL fetching with automatic CAPTCHA solving, markdown extraction, ~500 pre-built domain APIs, and remote browser infrastructure (150M+ IPs, thousands of concurrent sessions). A side-by-side comparison shows Walmart blocking plain requests while MCP succeeds. Token savings are quantified at roughly 62% for 90 products on one site, and approximately one million tokens saved for three Walmart pages; running scripts costs ~100 tokens versus ~10,000 for LLM-based parsing. Levi emphasizes that MCP is most useful for the ~20% of heavily protected domains (Akamai, Data Dome, Cloudflare)—often the most valuable data sources like real estate and large e-commerce. Bright Data only deals with public data, nothing behind login, citing lawsuits won against Meta and Twitter where judges ruled public data is public data. Agents can self-maintain: scheduled LLM checks validate data and repair broken selectors in about five minutes. Personal use cases include apartment-hunting and restaurant-booking listener scrapers. Remote browsers mimic real human behavior with pre-recorded mouse movements and typing patterns, making even lower-tier models like Claude Haiku sufficient for browsing agents.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Don't parse every page with an LLM—have the LLM build a reusable scraper script, saving massive token costs (~100 tokens vs ~10,000 for LLM parsing).
Bright Data's MCP provides 66 tools including curl-based fetching with CAPTCHA solving, scrape-as-markdown, ~500 pre-built domain APIs, and remote browser infrastructure with 150M+ IPs.
MCP is most valuable for the ~20% of heavily protected domains (Akamai, Data Dome, Cloudflare)—often the juiciest data sources like real estate and big e-commerce.
JSON output from scrapers is more token-efficient than markdown or HTML, further reducing costs.
Agents can self-heal pipelines: scheduled checks every 30 minutes validate data and auto-repair broken selectors in about 5 minutes, eliminating 2am human intervention.
Bright Data only handles public data—nothing behind login—and won lawsuits against Meta and Twitter establishing that public data collection is legal regardless of method.
Remote browsers mimic real human behavior with pre-recorded mouse movements and typing patterns, so even lower-tier models like Claude Haiku work for browsing agents.
Personal-scale use cases are practical: listener scrapers for apartment hunting and restaurant booking that run on schedules and notify or auto-act.
Agents can perform actions (fill forms, click buttons) on websites via remote browser, useful for sites where URLs can't be generated directly (e.g., flight searches).
A live demo built a working scraper for very.com in ~3 minutes; a Walmart comparison showed MCP bypassing bot-verification blocks successfully.

sections.title: Introduction: The Real Problem Is Maintenance, Not Scraping
sections.summary: Rafael Levi recaps the prior session on MCP bypassing CAPTCHA and bot detection, then frames this session's problem: collecting data at scale with LLMs without burning tokens. The key insight is to have the LLM build a scraper rather than parse every page. He describes the pain of maintaining scrapers when sites change selectors or use React, and introduces the concept of agents that explore, write, run, and maintain scrapers autonomously.

sections.title: Demo Setup: Claude Code and Bright Data Skills
sections.summary: Levi introduces Claude Code as his preferred coding agent and points to Bright Data's GitHub skills page containing scrape-builder best practices. He initiates a demo requesting a scraper for walmart.com with keyword search and max pages inputs, explaining the agent will fetch skills, use MCP to extract HTML, find selectors, and build the scraper. He notes scrape-as-markdown returns text only, not HTML tags, and that MCP offers 5,000 free requests.

sections.title: Token Savings Rationale and Personal Use Cases
sections.summary: Levi explains that building a scraper and using a script to parse HTML saves about a million tokens for three Walmart pages compared to LLM-based parsing. He describes personal use cases like finding best headphones by scanning marketplace reviews, and apartment hunting via a listener scraper that runs every 30 minutes and sends notifications—demonstrating utility beyond large-scale production scraping.

sections.title: Live Demo: Building a Scraper for Very.com
sections.summary: After an aborted Walmart attempt, an audience member suggests very.com (UK). Levi runs a clean demo: the agent builds a scraper for headphones across pages. He discusses Bright Data's 150M+ IPs, unlocking technology, and remote browser infrastructure capable of running thousands of browser sessions on their servers. The scraper collects 90 products and needs a Unicode fix for pound symbols.

sections.title: MCP Deep Dive: 66 Tools, Pre-built APIs, and CAPTCHA Solving
sections.summary: Responding to an audience question, Levi details the MCP's 66 tools: curl-style URL fetching with automatic CAPTCHA solving and correct headers/cookies; scrape-as-markdown for token-efficient text extraction; ~500 pre-built domain APIs (e.g., Amazon) returning JSON directly; and remote browser infrastructure. The system makes the server think requests come from a real browser.

sections.title: Comparison: With vs. Without MCP on Walmart
sections.summary: Levi demonstrates Walmart headphone search without MCP—blocked by a robot/human verification screen. With Bright Data MCP using scrape-as-markdown, the agent successfully retrieves product listings including the first result (blue headphones) with full product name. He then requests a token breakdown showing ~62% savings for 90 products, noting results vary by site structure, and emphasizes the agent will maintain and auto-repair the scraper if it breaks.

sections.title: Generated Code Review, Token Efficiency, and Public Data Legal Stance
sections.summary: Levi shows the generated scraper code: a parser using API web unlocker, output schema, keyword search and max pages inputs. He runs a second query for laptops. JSON output is highlighted as more token-efficient than markdown—running scripts costs ~100 tokens vs ~10,000 for LLM parsing. An audience question about authorization sites prompts Levi to clarify Bright Data only handles public data, nothing behind login. He cites lawsuits won against Meta and Twitter where judges ruled public data is public data regardless of collection method, while warning that accepting terms and conditions creates legal risk.

sections.title: Self-Healing Pipelines and MCP's Target Use Case
sections.summary: Levi summarizes the self-healing pipeline concept: agents with MCP access to blocked websites can build and maintain scrapers autonomously. He notes MCP is most useful for ~20% of domains with heavy protection (Akamai, Data Dome, Cloudflare)—typically the most valuable data sources like real estate and large e-commerce. Personal use cases are revisited: apartment hunting listeners and restaurant booking listeners that auto-act when spots open.

sections.title: Browser Actions, Human Mimicry, and Closing
sections.summary: Levi confirms agents can perform actions on websites—filling forms, clicking buttons—via remote browser, useful for sites where URLs can't be generated (e.g., flight searches). Remote browsers mimic real human behavior with pre-recorded mouse movements and typing patterns, making even Claude Haiku sufficient for browsing. He invites LinkedIn connections and booth visits, closes with 'keep the public data public.'
